position_in_era.historical_role: Pre-anchor riff blueprint: Jack Bruce's descending tritone-adjacent bass riff in D, doubled by Eric Clapton's guitar, established the 'riff-first' compositional contract in which the instrumental hook, not a chord sequence or melodic line, governs the song's identity. Pete Brown and Jack Bruce wrote the riff after a late-night session; Clapton arrived and locked in immediately — the riff came before the song.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded August 1967 at Atlantic Studios, New York, produced by Felix Pappalardi and Tom Dowd. The bass riff was written by Jack Bruce; Clapton doubled it on guitar in the intro and verse, creating the signature unison attack. Ginger Baker's shuffle drum pattern locks to the riff rather than the vocal — the percussion serves the riff.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Bruce (bass, lead vocal) and Clapton (guitar) co-own the riff equally — neither is subservient. Clapton's improvised solo in the middle section is the song's departure from and return to the riff-world. Baker's drums are structural glue rather than a competing voice.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Clapton: Gibson SG 'The Fool' through a Marshall stack; Bruce: Fender Bass VI; Baker: Ludwig drums. The riff is played at the octave on both instruments, giving it unusual low-register weight for a 1967 pop single.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Reached #36 US (1968 re-release) and #25 UK. Clapton has cited it as the song where Cream found their identity: riff-centred, heavy, improvisatory. Jimi Hendrix reportedly told them he loved the song after hearing it live at the Saville Theatre.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Single released November 1967 (US), January 1968 (UK). The song pre-dates Black Sabbath's self-titled track by three years and establishes the descending-riff grammar that Geezer Butler and Tony Iommi would radicalise.
